He publicly condemned the Warsaw Pact's 1968 invasion of Czechoslovakia, yet ruled Romania with an iron grip until his execution on Christmas Day 1989 — which communist leader?
Nicolae Ceaușescu: Leader of Romania from 1965 to 1989.
An English farmer-turned-soldier, he became a leading advocate for the 1649 execution of Charles I and then ruled as Lord Protector until his death in 1658 — who was he?
Oliver Cromwell: English military and political leader (1599–1658)
This American televangelist and onetime presidential candidate founded the Christian Broadcasting Network and Regent University across a five-decade career — who was he?
Pat Robertson: American media mogul and minister (1930–2023)
These seafaring Semitic traders sprang from the Bronze Age Canaanites and spread from Lebanon's coast all the way to Iberia, leaving thousands of inscriptions — what was their civilization called?

Founded by one of Alexander the Great's generals who declared himself pharaoh in 305 BC, this Macedonian Greek royal house ruled Egypt for 275 years until Rome absorbed it in 30 BC — which dynasty is it?

Ptolemaic dynasty: Macedonian Greek royal family which ruled Egypt. Reigning for 275 years, the Ptolemaic was the longest and last dynasty of ancient Egypt from 305 BC until its incorporation into the Roman Republic in 30 BC.
Ruling in medieval Delhi from 1236 to 1240, this daughter of Shamsuddin Iltutmish became the only female Muslim monarch to ever hold the throne there — who was she?
Razia Sultan: Raziyyat-Ud-Dunya Wa Ud-Din (Persian: سلطان رضیه الدنیا والدین; c.
The longest-serving prime minister in his nation's history, this Melbourne lawyer led one party in the 1930s and then founded an entirely new one for his second, much longer stint — who was he?
Robert Menzies: Prime Minister of Australia (1939–1941; 1949–1966)
In 2016, a former care-home employee killed 19 disabled residents in Kanagawa Prefecture, Japan, in the deadliest mass stabbing the country had seen in decades — what is this attack called?
Sagamihara stabbings: 2016 hate crime in Japan.
These horse-mounted nomads swept out of Central Asia to dominate the Pontic Steppe by the 8th century BC, later raiding West Asia after crossing the Caucasus — who were they?
Scythians: Nomadic Iranic people of the Pontic Steppe.
Serving five separate terms as prime minister between 1995 and 2022, this long-time Nepali Congress leader saw his tenure dogged by accusations of nepotism and corruption — who is he?
Founded in Japan in 1930 and rooted in the teachings of the 13th-century monk Nichiren, this Buddhist organization centers its practice on chanting a specific mantra — what is it?
Soka Gakkai: Japanese Buddhist religious movement.

At 25 she became Haryana's youngest-ever cabinet minister, and in 1998 she made history as Delhi's first female chief minister — who was this Indian diplomat who later ran external affairs under Modi?
This Thai telecom tycoon founded the mobile operator AIS, became one of the country's richest people, then won a landslide to become prime minister in 2001 — until a 2006 coup. Who is he?
Thaksin Shinawatra: Prime Minister of Thailand from 2001 to 2006.
Born Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, this British far-right activist co-founded and led the English Defence League from 2009 to 2013 — by what better-known name does he go?

Tommy Robinson: British far-right activist (born 1982). Stephen Christopher Yaxley-Lennon (né Yaxley; born 27 November 1982), better known as Tommy Robinson, is a British far-right, counter-jihad activist.
A combat veteran of the Second Chechen War who once commanded the 58th Combined Arms Army, he has run the General Staff of Russia's Armed Forces since 2012. Which Russian general is this?

Led by oligarch Yevgeny Prigozhin after months of feuding with Russia's defense minister over the war in Ukraine, this June 2023 uprising by a private military company ended a day later with Prigozhin standing down — what was it?
Wagner Group rebellion: 2023 Russian factional conflict.
The only person ever to lead both branches, this Skull and Bones member from Cincinnati served as the 27th U.S. president and later as Chief Justice of the United States — who is it?
William Howard Taft: President of the United States from 1909 to 1913.
The first hereditary successor to the caliphate, this second Umayyad caliph saw the death of Muhammad's grandson Husayn and the start of the Second Fitna during his reign — who was he?
Yazid I: Umayyad caliph from 680 to 683.
Before becoming Colombia's 32nd president in 2002, this leader of the right-wing Democratic Center party served as mayor of Medellín, then governor of Antioquia — who is he?
Álvaro Uribe: President of Colombia from 2002 to 2010.
Who among these was born first?
Calouste Gulbenkian (born 1869) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four was born earliest?
Maria Goeppert Mayer (born 1906) is the earliest of the four. In 1986, the Maria Goeppert Mayer Award for early-career women physicists was established in her honor.
Which of these four was founded earliest?

Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four. Fortran (formerly FORTRAN) is a third-generation, compiled, imperative programming language designed for numeric computation and scientific computing.
Which of these four dates back furthest?
MUMPS (founded 1966) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is a physicist?
Samuel C. C. Ting is a physicist.
Pick the chemist from these four.
What is the atomic number of Lawrencium?
Lawrencium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Lr (formerly Lw) and atomic number 103.
In what year was Hypatia born?
Hypatia: Not the only fourth century Alexandrian female mathematician, Hypatia was preceded by Pandrosion.
In what year was Bertrand Russell born?
Bertrand Russell: Bertrand Arthur William Russell, 3rd Earl Russell (18 May 1872 – 2 February 1970), was an English philosopher, logician, mathematician, and public intellectual.
In what year was Ümit Özdağ born?
Ümit Özdağ: On 16 November 2020, Özdağ was also dismissed from the Good Party.
In what year did Hans Albert Einstein die?
Hans Albert Einstein (May 14, 1904 – July 26, 1973) was a Swiss-American engineer, the second child and first son of physicists Albert Einstein and Mileva Marić.
In what year did John McAfee die?
John McAfee: In 1987, he wrote the first commercial anti-virus software, founding McAfee Associates to sell his creation.
In what year was Special relativity discovered?
Special relativity: In physics, the special theory of relativity, or simply special relativity, is a scientific theory of the relationship between space and time.
In what year was Mustard gas discovered?
Mustard gas: There is no preventive agent against mustard gas, with protection depending entirely on skin and airways protection, and no antidote exists for mustard poisoning.
Sodium acetate: Pfizer. Sodium acetate is a chemical compound with formula CH3COONa, also abbreviated NaOAc.
Which country is Northrop Grumman B-21 Raider from?

Northrop Grumman B-21 Raider: United States. Part of the Long Range Strike Bomber (LRS-B) program, it is to be an intercontinental strategic bomber that can deliver conventional and thermonuclear weapons.
Who is credited with discovering Archaea?
Archaea: Carl Woese. Archaea (ar-KEE-ə) is a domain of organisms.
Who is credited with discovering Synapse?
Synapse: Charles Scott Sherrington. In the nervous system, a synapse is a structure that allows a neuron to exchange (receive or send) signals with another cell in its immediate vicinity.
Who is credited with discovering Nitrogen?
Nitrogen: Daniel Rutherford. Nitrogen is a chemical element; it has symbol N and atomic number 7.
Known by the abbreviation NAC, this mucolytic drug treats acetaminophen overdose and also loosens thick mucus in people with chronic lung conditions like pneumonia and bronchitis — which drug?

Acetylcysteine (NAC) is a mucolytic that is used to treat paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose and to loosen thick mucus in individuals with chronic bronchopulmonary disorders, such as pneumonia and bronchitis.
Believed to be an autoimmune attack that breaches the immune privilege of hair follicles, this condition typically leaves a few coin-sized bald spots on the scalp — what is it?
Alopecia areata (AA), also known as spot baldness, is a condition in which hair is lost from some or all areas of the body.
Best known for his laws of planetary motion, this German astronomer has also been called the 'father of science fiction' for his novel Somnium. Who is he?

Antelope is any of the extant or recently extinct species of the ruminant artiodactyl family Bovidae, which are indigenous to most of Africa, India, the Middle East, Central Asia, and a small area of Russia.
Doctors reach for this NSAID not just for aches but to treat Kawasaki disease and rheumatic fever — and it's famous for its blood-thinning effect on platelets. What is it?
Aspirin is the genericized trademark for acetylsalicylic acid (ASA), a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) used to reduce pain, fever, and inflammation, and as an antithrombotic.

Found naturally in many plants and abbreviated "Bz," this white crystalline compound is the simplest of the aromatic carboxylic acids and lends its salts to the world of food preservatives — what is it?
Benzoic acid is a white or colorless crystalline organic compound with the formula C6H5COOH, whose structure consists of a benzene ring (C6H6) with a carboxyl (C(=O)OH) substituent.
This Russian mathematician-turned-oligarch was worth an estimated $3 billion in 1997 after privatizing state assets like Channel One — yet died impoverished and depressed in 2013. Who was he?
Boris Berezovsky (businessman) (23 January 1946 - 23 March 2013), also known as Platon Elenin, was a Russian business oligarch, government official, engineer and mathematician.
Atomic number 20 and chemically akin to strontium and barium, this metal is the most common ingredient in limestone — found there as its carbonate. What element?
Calcium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ca and atomic number 20.
A first-generation cephalosporin that can be swallowed rather than infused, this antibiotic disrupts the bacterial cell wall to treat ear, skin and urinary infections — what is it?
Cefalexin is an antibiotic that can treat a number of bacterial infections. It kills gram-positive and some gram-negative bacteria by disrupting the growth of the bacterial cell wall.
Charted in 1756 by Lacaille and named for the drafting tool that draws circles, this faint southern constellation is easily confused with the mariner's-compass constellation Pyxis. Which one is it?
Circinus is a small, faint constellation in the southern sky, first defined in 1756 by the French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille.
First created in Germany in 1996 and named for an astronomer on his 537th birthday, this synthetic element (number 112) may even be a gas — which one?
Copernicium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Cn and atomic number 112.

Known for names like thornapple, jimsonweed, and devil's trumpet, this genus of nine extremely poisonous, night-blooming plants in the nightshade family can cause hallucinations and delirium if ingested — what is it?
Datura is a genus of nine species of highly poisonous, vespertine-flowering plants belonging to the nightshade family (Solanaceae).
Its name comes from the Ancient Greek for 'female dragon,' and this genus of roughly 200 tree and shrub species now also includes what was once classified as Sansevieria — which genus is it?
Dracaena (plant) is a genus of about 200-220 species of trees and woody shrubs.
This branch of medicine studies the body's hormone-secreting glands and the chemical messengers, called hormones, that regulate growth, metabolism, mood, and more — name the field?
Endocrinology (from endocrine + -ology) is a branch of biology and medicine dealing with the endocrine system, its diseases, and its specific secretions known as hormones.
This Chinese-born American computer scientist built ImageNet, the dataset that supercharged computer vision in the 2010s, and co-directs Stanford's Human-Centered AI institute — who is she?

Fei-Fei Li (pinyin: L Fifi; born July 3, 1976) is a Chinese-born American computer scientist best known for establishing ImageNet, the dataset that enabled rapid advances in computer vision in the 2010s.
Named after a German militant group in a reader's 1994 letter and formalized by a Stanford linguist in 2005, this cognitive bias makes newly learned facts seem suddenly everywhere — what is it?

Frequency illusion (also known as the Baader-Meinhof phenomenon or Red Car Theory) is a cognitive bias in which a person notices a specific concept, word, or product more frequently after recently becoming aware of it.
The largest and outermost of the three hip muscles, this one shapes the buttocks and helps keep the human trunk upright — what muscle is it?
Gluteus maximus is the main extensor muscle of the hip in humans.

Element 108's isotope 270 carries magic numbers of protons and neutrons that shore it up against fission, yet the most stable forms last only about ten seconds — which synthetic superheavy element is it?
Hassium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Hs and atomic number 108.
Running from the shoulder to the elbow, this arm bone connects the scapula to the radius and ulna, with a rounded head and neck at one end and two epicondyles at the other — name this bone?
Humerus (pl.: humeri) is a long bone in the arm that runs from the shoulder to the elbow.
Denoted by the symbol ∞, this concept of the boundless and endless has been debated by philosophers since ancient Greece and by mathematicians since the 17th century — what is it?
Infinity is something which is boundless, limitless, or endless.
Known as the sunroot or earth apple, this central-North-American member of the sunflower family is cultivated for its tuber rather than its bloom — what is it?
Jerusalem artichoke (Helianthus tuberosus), also called sunroot, sunchoke, wild sunflower, topinambur, or earth apple, is a species of sunflower native to central North America.
Native to Central and South American rainforests, this frugivorous nocturnal mammal related to raccoons and coatis shares its 'honey bear' nickname with an unrelated species — which animal?
Kinkajou (/kkdu/; Potos flavus) is a mammal of the family Procyonidae, a relative to olingos, coatis, raccoons, and the ringtail and cacomistle.
Used to treat an underactive thyroid and even a severe form called myxedema coma, this synthetic version of thyroxine (T4) takes about six weeks to reach a steady blood level — what's this drug?
Levothyroxine is a synthetic form of the thyroid hormone thyroxine (T4). It is used to treat thyroid hormone deficiency (hypothyroidism), including a severe form known as myxedema coma.
The sole species in its genus, this South Chinese fruit has a sweet, mildly tart flavor and a distinctive rose-like floral aroma — name it?
Lychee (US also) are the fruit of the tree Litchi chinensis, the sole member of the genus Litchi, part of the soapberry family, Sapindaceae.
In hermaphroditic species this reproductive pairing isn't strictly required, since self-fertilization is possible — what is the general term for it?
Mating refers to the pairing of either opposite-sex or hermaphroditic organisms for the purpose of sexual reproduction.
First flown by the Soviet Air Force in 1968 and still in Russian production today, this medium chopper carries the NATO reporting name 'Hip' — what aircraft is it?
Mil Mi-8 is a family of medium twin-turbine helicopters, originally designed by the Soviet Central Aerohydrodynamic Institute (TsAGI) in the 1960s and introduced into the Soviet Air Force in 1968.

Caused when fly larvae burrow into and feed on an animal's tissue, this parasitic infestation is triggered by open wounds but can occur on unbroken skin when species such as the botfly are involved — name this condition?
Myiasis (my-), also known as flystrike or fly strike, is the parasitic infestation of the body of a live animal by fly larvae (maggots) that grow inside the host while feeding on its tissue.
This Danish-Norwegian eurodance group's 1997 single caused controversy and a lawsuit from a toy company over its double entendres about a certain plastic doll. Who are they?
North American XB-70 Valkyrie is a retired prototype version of the planned B-70 nuclear-armed, deep-penetration supersonic strategic bomber for the United States Air Force Strategic Air Command.
Making up most of Earth's crust, this class of chemical compounds pairs oxygen with at least one other element — even the thin protective skin on aluminum foil counts as one — what's the class?
Oxide is a chemical compound containing at least one oxygen atom and one other element in its chemical formula.

Classically, one form of this condition wakes you at night with upper abdominal pain that eases when you eat, while another flares up after meals — and a third of older sufferers feel nothing at all. What is it?
Peptic ulcer disease refers to damage of the inner part of the stomach's gastric mucosa (lining of the stomach), the first part of the small intestine, or sometimes the lower esophagus.
This GABA-derived drug treats cognitive disorders, vertigo, and dyslexia, and shares its 'racetam' drug class with related compounds like levetiracetam and aniracetam — what is it?
Piracetam is a drug that has efficacy in cognitive disorders, vertigo, cortical myoclonus, dyslexia, and sickle cell anemia; sources differ on its usefulness for dementia.
Bloating, mood swings, breast tenderness and irritability that flare in the week or two before menstruation and fade once bleeding begins — what disruptive condition is this?
Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) is a disruptive set of emotional and physical symptoms that regularly occur in the one to two weeks before the start of each menstrual period.
This colorless, odorless radioactive noble gas has the atomic number 86, and its longest-lived isotope has a half-life of under four days — name the element?
Radon is a chemical element; it has symbol Rn and atomic number 86.

Usually hidden below the soil surface but sometimes growing aerial or aerating instead, these plant organs anchor a plant while drawing in the water and nutrients it needs to grow taller and faster — name them?
Root are the organs of a plant that are modified to provide anchorage for the plant and take in water and nutrients into the plant body, which allows plants to grow taller and faster.
Which leathery-skinned marine echinoderm, of which about 1,786 species are known worldwide, plays a vital ecological role on the sea floor by breaking down detritus as a scavenger?
Sea cucumber are echinoderms from the class Holothuroidea.
Unlike its shelled cousin the snail, this soft-bodied land mollusk gets by with no shell at all, or at most a tiny internal remnant of one — what animal is it?
Slug is a common name for any apparently shell-less terrestrial gastropod mollusc.
Built from four fused rings, compounds in this class include cholesterol, testosterone, and anti-inflammatory drugs like dexamethasone. What class of compound is it?
Steroid is an organic compound with four fused rings (designated A, B, C, and D) arranged in a specific molecular configuration.
One of the oldest constellations, this zodiac figure once marked the Sun's place at the spring equinox and inspired bull imagery from Sumer to Rome — which northern-sky constellation is it?
Taurus (constellation) (Latin, 'Bull') is one of the constellations of the zodiac and is located in the northern celestial hemisphere.
Found in nature only as an oxide and locked in minerals like rutile and ilmenite, this strong, silvery element bears the name of mythological giants — what is it?
Titanium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ti and atomic number 22.

An oily, amber-colored liquid that's extremely non-volatile and therefore lingers in the environment, this organophosphorus compound was developed for chemical warfare and is lethal in doses of just tens of milligrams — which chemical agent?
VX (nerve agent) is an extremely toxic synthetic chemical compound in the organophosphorus class, specifically, a thiophosphonate.
Native to Eastern and Southern Africa, this large antelope genus includes two species — one black, one blue — whose lineages diverged roughly a million years ago — what animal is it?
Wildebeest (VIL-), also called gnu (NOO or, NEW), are antelopes of the genus Connochaetes and native to Eastern and Southern Africa.

These ear-shaped sea snails wear a shell with a row of breathing holes and a pearly inside, and their flesh is prized as a delicacy worldwide — about 70 species, the biggest a foot long. What are they?
Abalone: Common name for a group of sea snails.
One of the world's few semiaquatic vipers, this venomous pit viper of the southeastern United States coils and displays its fangs when threatened — what is it?
This genus of over 650 succulent species includes a 'true' member long used in pharmaceutical products, native to Africa, Madagascar, and the Arabian Peninsula — which genus?
Aloe: Genus of succulent flowering plants.
Despite helping develop the Soviet Union's thermonuclear weapons, this physicist won the 1975 Nobel Peace Prize for his human-rights activism and was later persecuted as a dissident — who was he?
Andrei Sakharov: Soviet nuclear physicist and human rights activist (1921–1989)
In this severe blood disorder, the bone marrow stops producing red cells, white cells and platelets alike, and about half of all cases have no known cause — what condition is it?
Aplastic anemia: Disease causing insufficient blood cells of all types.

One of its founders, James Keeler, said this science 'seeks to ascertain the nature of the heavenly bodies... rather than their positions or motions' — studying everything from the Sun to the cosmic microwave background. What field is it?
Sitting at the bottom of the forebrain and including the striatum and substantia nigra, this cluster of brain nuclei governs voluntary movement and habit formation — what is it called?
Basal ganglia: Group of subcortical nuclei involved in the motor and reward systems.
Coined by Károly Ereky in 1919, this multidisciplinary field harnesses bacteria, yeast, and plants — often via genetic engineering — to create products and services. What field?
Biotechnology: Use of living systems and organisms to develop or make useful products.
Certified in Canada in 1998, this large-cabin business jet shares its fuselage cross-section with the Challenger 600 and first flew in 1996 — which jet is it?
Bombardier Global Express: Large cabin business jet. The Bombardier Global Express is a large cabin, long-range business jet designed and manufactured by Bombardier Aviation.

Comprising over 250 species that form small colonies of as few as 50 individuals around a single queen, these fuzzy insects were introduced to New Zealand and Tasmania and can sting repeatedly without dying — which insect is it?
Bumblebee: Genus of insect. A bumblebee (or bumble bee, bumble-bee, or humble-bee) is any of over 250 species in the genus Bombus, part of Apidae, one of the bee families.
Designated Alpha Carinae and located some 310 light-years away, this bright giant is the second-brightest star in the night sky, outshone only by Sirius — which star?
Canopus: Brightest star in the constellation of Carina.
A first-generation cephalosporin and β-lactam, this antibiotic can be taken by mouth and treats ear, bone, skin and urinary infections by disrupting bacterial cell-wall growth — what is it?
Cefalexin: Beta-lactam antibiotic. Cefalexin, also spelled cephalexin, is an antibiotic that can treat a number of bacterial infections.
Nicknamed the sea wasp, this Australian box jellyfish is considered the world's most lethal, with venom-laced tentacles up to 10 feet long — which species?
Chironex fleckeri: Species of jellyfish. It has been described as "the most lethal jellyfish in the world", with at least 64 known deaths in Australia from 1884 to 2021.
Discovered in 1969 and sold under the brand name Lotrimin, this azole-class medication treats athlete's foot, ringworm, and oral thrush — what is it?

Native to the western Palearctic and closely related to the rock dove, this large bird feeds mainly on cereals and other plant matter, making it an agricultural pest despite being heavily hunted across its range — what is it?
Common wood pigeon: Species of large, white/green-naped, arboreal bird of Eurasia.
This genus of some 100 low-growing perennials gives us saffron from the dried stigmas of one autumn-blooming species — name the flower genus?
This basic unit of time — averaging 24 hours, or 86,400 seconds — marks one full rotation of the Earth relative to the Sun, and got split into weeks, months, and years. What is it?
Day: Time of one rotation around a planet axis.

Governed since 1961 by the Vienna Convention, this practice of using official representatives to influence international relations became a professionalized field in the early 20th century. What is it?
Diplomacy: Practice of conducting negotiations between representatives of groups or states.
This condition involves involuntarily repeating words or sounds spoken by someone else, and is commonly seen in autism, ADHD, and Tourette syndrome. What is it called?
This branch of zoology, whose name derives from Greek words for 'insect' and 'study,' covers a field that has described over 1.3 million species — which discipline?
The only Old World member of its family to breed in the Northern Hemisphere's temperate zones, this migratory songbird winters in central and southern Africa — what is it?
Eurasian golden oriole: Species of bird.
This Austrian-German automotive engineer built the first gasoline-electric hybrid car and designed the Volkswagen Beetle, but also contributed tanks to Nazi Germany's war effort — who was he?
Ferdinand Porsche: Austrian-born German automotive engineer, inventor (1875–1951)
A type of necrotizing tissue infection affecting the genitals or perineum, this condition most often strikes older men, diabetics or the immunocompromised — what is it called?
Fournier gangrene: Medical condition. It most commonly occurs in older men, but it can also occur both in women and children, diabetics, alcoholics, or the immunocompromised.
Commonly known as snails and slugs, this class is the second-largest in the animal kingdom after insects — what is it called?
Gastropod: Class of molluscs. The fossil record of gastropods extends back to the Late Cambrian.

A colorless, sweet-tasting, syrupy liquid, this sugar alcohol carries three hydroxyl groups, forms the backbone of triglycerides in fats and oils, and doubles as a food-industry sweetener. What is it?

Once nearly all lumped into a single genus before 21st-century research proved that grouping polyphyletic, these grey-and-white seabirds have an older dialect name, 'mew,' echoing their calls — which birds?
Gull: Subfamily of seabirds. The large species take up to four years to attain full adult plumage, but two years is typical for small gulls.
This medical term describes red blood cells rupturing and spilling their contents into the plasma — a process triggered by bacterial toxins or even intense exercise. What is it?
Hemolysis: Rupturing of red blood cells and release of their contents. Hemolysis may occur in vivo or in vitro.
Often called the founder of alpinism and modern meteorology, this Genevan scientist is also credited with building the first successful solar oven — who was he?
Horace Bénédict de Saussure: Genevan scientist and mountaineer (1740–1799)
Marked by dizziness, blurred vision, and fatigue, this cardiovascular condition is generally diagnosed when systolic readings fall under 90 mmHg — what is it?
This ring-shaped structure in the eye controls how much light reaches the retina by adjusting the size of the pupil — and it's also what determines eye color — what is it?
Iris (anatomy): Colored part of an eye.
Once a deputy district attorney in Weld County, Colorado, this now-suspended lawyer served on Donald Trump's 2020 campaign legal team — who is she?
A genus of roughly 125 succulent species native mostly to Madagascar, one of its members became one of the first plants ever sent into space, aboard a Soviet resupply mission in 1979 — which genus?
Kalanchoe: Genus of flowering plants in the stonecrop family.
Named from Greek words for 'hare' and 'form,' this mammalian order splits into rabbits-and-hares on one branch and pikas on the other, totaling around 110 living species — which order?
Cell signaling, homeostasis, metabolism, growth and reproduction are its hallmarks — and every instance of it eventually reaches death. What capacity in matter is this?
This French chemist's discoveries in fermentation and vaccination gave us a heat-treatment process that now bears his name and rabies and anthrax vaccines — who was he?
Louis Pasteur: French chemist, pharmacist and microbiologist (1822–1895)
In larger organizations it stacks into a pyramid, with a board and CEO at the top setting strategy — the broad practice of administering a business or government. What is it?
Management: Coordinating the efforts of persons.
Diagnosis, prognosis, prevention, treatment and palliation of injury and disease — drawing on biomedical science, genetics and technology — define this science and practice. What is it?

Medicine: Diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of illness. Medicine encompasses a variety of health care practices which evolved to maintain and restore health through the prevention and treatment of illness and infection.
This theoretical physicist and science communicator bridged science and science fiction well enough to win a 2021 lifetime achievement award named for Arthur C. Clarke — who is he?
Michio Kaku: American theoretical physicist, futurist and author.

There's a large introduced population of this small carnivorous mammal in Hawaii, though its family — split into the Herpestinae and Mungotinae — is native to southern Europe, Africa, and Asia — what animal is it?

Mongoose: Family of mammals in Africa and Asia. The Herpestinae comprises 23 living species that are native to southern Europe, Africa and Asia, whereas the Mungotinae comprises 11 species native to Africa.
Named for its resemblance to a tiny mouse's ear, this flowering plant genus is known in the Northern Hemisphere by a romantic common name and is Alaska's official flower — what is it?
Myosotis: Genus of flowering plants in the family Boraginaceae.
This synthetic element 113 was claimed by both a Russian-American team at Dubna and, in 2004, a Japanese team at Riken. What's its name?
Nihonium: Chemical element with atomic number 113 (Nh)
Sold under the brand name Zyprexa, this atypical antipsychotic treats schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, and is sometimes used off-label to fight chemotherapy-induced nausea — what is this drug?
Olanzapine: Atypical antipsychotic medication. Olanzapine, sold under the brand name Zyprexa among others, is an atypical antipsychotic primarily used to treat schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.
Prized both as a delicacy and, in some species, for the pearls grown within its shell, which salt-water bivalve is this?
Oyster: Variety of families of Mollusca.
This hickory species native to the Mississippi River region produces a nut used in praline candy and a famous holiday pie, and is the official state tree of Texas — what is it?
Pecan: Species of nut tree native to the southern USA and northern Mexico.
The body produces about a quart of this substance daily to trap airborne particles and bacteria — coughed up, it's also known as sputum. What is it?
Phlegm: Mucus produced by the respiratory system (excluding the nasal passages)
Downgraded from planet to dwarf in 2006 when astronomers adopted a new definition, this Kuiper belt object orbits beyond Neptune—what celestial body is it?
Pluto: Largest dwarf planet. Pluto (minor-planet number 134340) is a dwarf planet in the Kuiper belt, a ring of bodies beyond the orbit of Neptune.
Sold under the brand name Phenergan, this first-generation antihistamine treats allergies and nausea but has also seen recreational misuse alongside codeine — which drug?
Promethazine: Sedating antihistamine. Promethazine is taken by mouth (oral), as a rectal suppository, or by injection into a muscle (IM).
Once one of America's leading rocket experts with an MIT aeronautics degree, he was deported to China in 1955 and went on to father that nation's space program — which aerospace engineer?

Nicknamed the 'Jug,' this WWII American fighter-bomber carried eight .50-caliber machine guns and weighed up to eight tons fully loaded, making it one of the heaviest fighters of the war — which aircraft?

Republic P-47 Thunderbolt: Family of fighter aircraft. The Republic P-47 Thunderbolt (nicknamed the "Jug") is a World War II-era fighter aircraft produced by the American company Republic Aviation from 1941 through 1945.

A Mediterranean shrub in the mint family, this plant bears fragrant, needle-like evergreen leaves and purple, white, pink, or blue flowers — and those leaves are a beloved cooking flavoring. What is it?
Rosemary: Species of plant. It has numerous cultivars, and its leaves are commonly used as a flavoring.
